subject: Automotive & EVs
title: Pedestrian Safety Design
description: Learn Pedestrian Safety Design in one minute.

hook.text: For decades, car safety focused entirely on the people inside the car, not outside it.

buildup.text: Pedestrians struck by boxy hoods and rigid bumpers suffered devastating head and leg injuries.

discovery.text: Euro NCAP began scoring pedestrian protection, forcing designers to soften front-end shapes.

twist.text: Modern hoods dent easily on impact—some even pop up to cushion a pedestrian's head.

climax.text: Volvo introduced an external pedestrian airbag in 2012, deploying at the windshield base.

punchline.text: Cars are now designed to protect the people they hit.

quiz.question: Why do some modern car hoods pop up during a collision?
options: To cushion a pedestrian's head on impact

details.summary: Modern cars are designed with energy-absorbing hoods, softer bumpers, and external airbags to reduce injuries when a vehicle strikes a pedestrian, turning car design into pedestrian protection.
details.whyItMatters: Pedestrian fatalities remain a major road safety challenge. Design standards requiring deformable front structures have measurably reduced pedestrian head and leg injury severity.
takeaways: Raised hood lines create clearance from hard engine parts
Bumper shapes are optimized to reduce leg fracture severity
Some cars deploy external airbags over the windshield base

faq.question: How does raising the car hood help protect pedestrians?
faq.answer: A gap between the hood and engine allows the metal to deform on impact, cushioning the pedestrian's head. Without this space the head would hit unyielding engine components directly.

faq.question: Do SUVs pose a greater danger to pedestrians than sedans?
faq.answer: Yes. Taller front ends strike pedestrians higher on the body, hitting the chest or head instead of the legs. This increases the severity of injuries and fatality rates in pedestrian collisions.
